adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative: every token is in the ~1000 most frequent English word band the hypothesis says leaves the pole at 0, with no rare word, name, number or non-ASCII byte.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She said, "I can do it in a day if the people help me."
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative: a full sentence of frequent function and content words (can, do, day, people) in ordinary prose, which the token-rarity rule predicts stays inactive.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Battery is a word that can be on the table.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Position hard negative: the claimed trigger 'Battery' is the first token, which the hypothesis says is never active, and every later token is frequent.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The people had one or two of them in a year, and that was good for them.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative for the rare-number half of the rule: small numbers spelled as the frequent words 'one' and 'two' in ordinary prose, which the hypothesis says contribute 0.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: When the day was over they went back to the room and said it was good.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative: an all-frequent-word sentence with a different structure and a time-and-room topic, testing that ordinary prose without an unfamiliar token stays at 0.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: What can it do for the people of the year?
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative: a question built only from common words, testing that ordinary frequent-word text does not fire the rarity pole regardless of sentence type.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: One of the best ways to do it is to take a look and see for yourself.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative: an everyday idiom-like sentence of high-frequency words, probing whether the pole stays quiet without any genuinely uncommon token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The man in the room can see the water and the table.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative: keeps the top examples' lodging-and-facilities topic but uses only common words, separating the claimed rarity feature from the topic.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He said that a day on the bus can be a good day for the people.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative: frequent-word sentence containing several of the listed common words (day, bus, people, can) in ordinary context.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: There is no way to know the number of the year.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative: frequent words including 'number' and 'year' spelled out as common vocabulary, testing that the rarity rule does not fire on common number words.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: They went out from the room and came back to the same place.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative: another all-frequent-word sentence with different structure, checking the pole stays at 0 across varied common prose.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The people were on the bus for a day, and they could see the water from the room. It was a good year for them, and they said so to the man at the table. He did not know what to do about it, so he went out for a time. When he came back, the table was in the same place and the people were still there. They had a good time and they can do it again, just as they did on the first day.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long-context hard negative: a multi-sentence passage deep in the frequent-word band, testing that length alone does not wake the rarity pole.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The room has a bed and a table, and the people can see the water from it. They said it was good, and they will come back for a day in the year.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative: lodging topic with all common words, including frequent 'table' and 'day', testing the topic-without-rarity near-miss.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The xylophone rested beside the walnut cabinet in the vestibule.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Positive holdout: paraphrase of the rarity feature using uncommon English words (xylophone, walnut, vestibule) absent from the examples and from the listed common band.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Sales rose 47.3% between Q3 2019 and Q4 2020.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Positive holdout: rare numbers and abbreviations in a business context, one of the ASCII classes the hypothesis says saturates the pole.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Москва является столицей Российской Федерации, и город растёт.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Positive holdout: Cyrillic text, which the hypothesis says fires via non-ASCII byte pieces, in a language absent from the examples.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Η Αθήνα είναι η πρωτεύουσα της Ελλάδας και της Αττικής.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Positive holdout: Greek script, another non-ASCII byte set the hypothesis claims saturates in 90-95% of occurrences.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Le café était près de la gare, où le père attendait son ami.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Positive holdout: accented Latin (é, è, ù) in French, testing the claim that any non-ASCII byte token fires even inside otherwise ordinary words.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: 東京は日本の首都であり、多くの人が住んでいます。
adversarial_test_results.detail: Positive holdout: CJK text with the claimed byte-piece tokens, in a genre and language unlike the multilingual wikipedia examples.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The table was set — and the people sat down.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Positive holdout for the byte rule: an em dash is a non-ASCII byte token, so the hypothesis predicts the pole fires even though every word is frequent.
